ref-phases.prompt: The most important table in the course. Learn it with the input and output columns, not just the names, because that is what turns a three mark list into a full answer.
ref-phases.solution:
#PhaseTakesProducesCatches
1Lexical analysis (scanning)Source charactersA stream of tokensIllegal characters, malformed identifiers
2Syntax analysis (parsing)TokensA parse tree or syntax treeGrammar violations, such as a missing semicolon or bracket
3Semantic analysisSyntax treeAnnotated syntax treeType mismatches, undeclared variables, wrong argument counts
4Intermediate code generationAnnotated treeIntermediate representation, such as three address codeNothing; this is a translation step
5Code optimisationIntermediate codeImproved intermediate codeNothing; it must preserve meaning exactly
6Code generationOptimised intermediate codeTarget machine or assembly codeNothing

Two activities run across all six rather than sitting inside one: symbol table management and error handling. Drawing them as vertical bars beside the phase diagram is exactly what the textbook figure does, and reproducing it earns the diagram mark.

The front end and back end split

Phases 1 to 4 are the front end, which depends on the source language and not on the target machine. Phases 5 and 6 are the back end, which depends on the target machine and not on the source language. That separation is why one front end can serve many machines and one back end many languages, which is the standard answer to "why is a compiler divided into phases".

ref-chomsky.prompt: Straight from CSC328, and it explains why a compiler has both a scanner and a parser instead of one machine doing everything.
ref-chomsky.solution:
TypeGrammarProduction formRecogniserUsed in a compiler for
3RegularA → aB or A → aFinite automatonLexical analysis: tokens
2Context-freeA → α, one non-terminal on the leftPushdown automatonSyntax analysis: program structure
1Context-sensitiveαAβ → αγβLinear bounded automatonNot used directly; the semantic phase handles what needs context
0Unrestrictedα → β, α not emptyTuring machineNot used

The question this table answers, which is asked often: why can a regular grammar not describe a whole programming language? Because a finite automaton has no memory beyond its current state, so it cannot count. It cannot check that every opening bracket has a matching closing bracket, since that requires remembering an unbounded number of them. A pushdown automaton has a stack, which is exactly the memory that matching brackets needs. So tokens are regular and program structure is context-free.

The follow-up: why is a context-free grammar not enough either? Because declaring a variable before use, and matching an argument's type to a parameter's type, are context conditions. Rather than move to a context-sensitive grammar, which would be impractical to parse, compilers check these in the semantic analysis phase instead.

ref-parsers.prompt: A single table that places every parser you will meet. Questions ask you to classify, to compare power, or to say why a given grammar fails a given parser.
ref-parsers.solution:
FamilyParserDirectionDerivationNotes
Top downRecursive descent with backtrackingLeft to rightLeftmostSimple to write by hand, but slow and cannot handle left recursion
LL(1), predictiveLeft to rightLeftmostNo backtracking; needs a grammar with no left recursion and no common prefixes
Bottom upOperator precedenceLeft to rightRightmost, in reverseOnly for operator grammars; simple and fast
LR(0), SLR(1)Left to rightRightmost, in reverseSLR uses FOLLOW sets to decide reductions; weakest of the LR family
LALR(1)Left to rightRightmost, in reverseMerges CLR states, so smaller tables; used by yacc and bison
CLR(1), canonical LRLeft to rightRightmost, in reverseMost powerful, largest tables

Power ordering, worth quoting: LR(0) ⊂ SLR(1) ⊂ LALR(1) ⊂ CLR(1), and every LL(1) grammar is also LR(1) but not the reverse. In one sentence: bottom up parsers handle strictly more grammars than top down parsers, which is why real compilers use them, and top down parsers are easier to write by hand, which is why courses teach them first.

What the letters mean, since it is a one mark question: in LL(1) the first L is scanning left to right, the second L is producing a leftmost derivation, and the 1 is the number of lookahead symbols. In LR(1) the R is a rightmost derivation, produced in reverse.

ref-terms.prompt: Two small definition sets that appear on almost every paper and take thirty seconds each if you know them exactly.
ref-terms.solution:
Token, pattern, lexeme

TermDefinitionExample
TokenA category of lexical unit, a name and optionally an attribute valueidentifier, number, relop
PatternThe rule describing the form a lexeme of that token may takeA letter followed by letters or digits

The one line that fixes the three: in total = count + 10, total and count are lexemes, both of the token identifier, matching the pattern "letter followed by letters or digits". Give exactly that example and the three definitions cannot be confused.

Compiler, interpreter, assembler and the rest

TranslatorTranslatesKey property
CompilerHigh level source into machine or object code, all at onceTranslation and execution are separate; errors are reported for the whole program before it runs
InterpreterExecutes the source statement by statementNo object code produced; stops at the first error; slower to run, faster to debug

ref-opt.prompt: "Name and illustrate five code optimisation techniques" is a standard question. The illustration is where the marks are, so learn one tiny example per technique rather than a definition.
ref-opt.solution:
TechniqueWhat it doesBefore → after
Constant foldingEvaluates constant expressions at compile timex = 4 * 5 → x = 20
Constant propagationReplaces a variable known to hold a constant with that constanta = 5; b = a + 2 → b = 7
Common subexpression eliminationComputes a repeated expression once and reuses itx = a*b + c; y = a*b + d → t = a*b; x = t + c; y = t + d
Dead code eliminationRemoves code whose result is never used or which can never runx = 5; x = 7; → the first assignment is removed
Strength reductionReplaces an expensive operation with a cheaper equivalentx = y * 2 → x = y + y, or a left shift
Loop invariant code motionMoves a computation that does not change out of the loopwhile(i<n){ x = a*b; ... } → compute a*b once before the loop
Loop unrollingRepeats the body to cut the number of tests and jumpsFour iterations become one body doing four items

The rule that governs every one of them, and the sentence to open the answer with: an optimisation must never change the meaning of the program. It may make it faster or smaller, but the output for any input must be identical. Optimisations are also classified as local, within one basic block, global, across blocks in a procedure, and machine dependent, exploiting the target's own instructions such as registers and addressing modes.

t1.prompt: A compiler is a program that reads a program written in one language, the source language, and translates it into an equivalent program in another language, the target language, reporting any errors it detects in the process.
t1.solution:
Note the two obligations inside that definition: producing an equivalent program, and reporting errors. A translator that produced fast but wrong code would not be a compiler, and neither would one that silently accepted invalid input.

Why divide it into phases at all

  • Manageability. Each phase solves one problem with one well defined input and output, so it can be written and tested alone.
  • Portability. The front end depends only on the source language and the back end only on the target machine, so m languages and n machines need m + n pieces rather than m × n complete compilers.
  • Optimisation. Working on a machine independent intermediate representation means one optimiser serves every target.
  • Reuse. Tools such as lex and yacc can generate whole phases from a specification.

The m + n against m × n argument is the strongest single point in any "why phases" answer, because it is concrete. With 4 languages and 5 machines you write 9 components instead of 20 compilers.

Single pass and multi pass

A pass reads the input representation once and produces an output representation. A single pass compiler completes translation in one traversal, which is fast and uses little memory but restricts the language, for example by requiring declaration before use. A multi pass compiler traverses several times, which allows more optimisation and more flexible language rules at the cost of speed and memory. Phases and passes are not the same thing: several phases can be folded into one pass.

Drill

  1. Define a compiler and state its two obligations. The definition above, with equivalence and error reporting.
  2. Differentiate a compiler from an interpreter. A compiler translates the whole program into object code before any of it runs, reports all errors together, and gives faster execution. An interpreter executes statement by statement, produces no object code, stops at the first error, and gives slower execution but easier debugging.
  3. Why is a compiler divided into phases? The four bullets, leading with m + n against m × n.
  4. Differentiate a phase from a pass. A phase is a logical stage of translation with a defined input and output; a pass is one complete reading of the program representation. Several phases may be combined into a single pass.

t2.prompt: The classic long question: "show what each phase of a compiler produces for the statement position = initial + rate * 60". It is worth full marks every time because the answer is fixed and mechanical.
t2.solution:
Phase 1, lexical analysis

The character stream becomes tokens, and each identifier is entered into the symbol table:

id1  =  id2  +  id3  *  60
Symbol table:  1 position    2 initial    3 rate

Phase 2, syntax analysis

The tokens are built into a syntax tree. Multiplication binds tighter than addition, so it sits deeper:

          =
/   \
id1    +
/   \
id2     *
/   \
id3     60

Phase 3, semantic analysis

Types are checked and coercions inserted. If position, initial and rate are reals and 60 is an integer, the compiler inserts a conversion:

          =
/   \
id1    +
/   \
id2     *
/   \
id3   inttoreal
|
60

Phase 4, intermediate code generation

t1 = inttoreal(60)
t2 = id3 * t1
t3 = id2 + t2
id1 = t3

Phase 5, code optimisation

The conversion of the constant 60 can be done at compile time, and t3 is used only once so it can be folded away:

t1 = id3 * 60.0
id1 = id2 + t1

Phase 6, code generation

MOVF  id3, R2
MULF  #60.0, R2
MOVF  id2, R1
ADDF  R2, R1
MOVF  R1, id1

Four bars run down the side of that diagram in every textbook: the symbol table manager and the error handler both touch every phase. Mention them or you lose a mark on an otherwise perfect answer.

Drill

  1. Trace a = b + c * 5 through all six phases. Same shape as above: tokens, tree with the multiply deeper, type check, four lines of three address code, optimised to two, then machine instructions.
  2. At which phase would each of these be caught? A missing semicolon: syntax analysis. Using an undeclared variable: semantic analysis. An illegal character such as @ in an identifier: lexical analysis. Assigning a string to an integer variable: semantic analysis.
  3. Why does the multiplication appear deeper in the syntax tree than the addition? Because the grammar encodes operator precedence: multiplication binds more tightly, so it is reduced first and therefore sits lower, which makes the tree evaluate it first.

t3.prompt: A context-free grammar is a four-tuple G = (V, T, P, S): a set of non-terminals V, a set of terminals T, a set of productions P, and a start symbol S.
t3.solution:
Derivations

A derivation is a sequence of production applications turning the start symbol into a string of terminals. In a leftmost derivation the leftmost non-terminal is replaced at each step; in a rightmost derivation the rightmost is.

Take the grammar E → E + E | E * E | id and derive id + id * id:

Leftmost:
E ⇒ E + E ⇒ id + E ⇒ id + E * E ⇒ id + id * E ⇒ id + id * id
Rightmost:
E ⇒ E + E ⇒ E + E * E ⇒ E + E * id ⇒ E + id * id ⇒ id + id * id

Both reach the same string by the same tree here, but the order of steps differs. Top down parsers produce leftmost derivations; bottom up parsers produce rightmost derivations in reverse.

Ambiguity

A grammar is ambiguous if some string has more than one parse tree, equivalently more than one leftmost derivation. The grammar above is ambiguous, because id + id * id has two trees:

Tree A: (id + id) * id        Tree B: id + (id * id)
*                             +
/   \                         /   \
+     id                     id     *
/   \                               /   \
id    id                            id    id

Ambiguity matters because the two trees compute different values. With id = 2, Tree A gives (2+2)*2 = 8 and Tree B gives 2+(2*2) = 6. A compiler cannot choose arbitrarily, so ambiguity must be removed. Giving that arithmetic is what turns a definition into an explanation.

It is removed either by rewriting the grammar so that precedence and associativity are built into its layers, as in T10, or by declaring precedence and associativity separately, which is what yacc does.

Drill

  1. Define a context-free grammar and name its four components. The four-tuple above with one example of each.
  2. Give the leftmost and rightmost derivations of id * id + id for the grammar above. Replace the leftmost or rightmost non-terminal at each step and show every step.
  3. Show that the grammar is ambiguous. Produce two distinct parse trees for one string, and note that they evaluate differently.
  4. State two ways of removing ambiguity. Rewriting the grammar into precedence levels, or supplying precedence and associativity declarations to the parser generator.

t4.prompt: The tools of the scanner. A regular expression describes a token's pattern; a finite automaton recognises it. The two are equivalent in power, which is the theorem the whole of lexical analysis rests on.
t4.solution:
The operations, in precedence order

OperationNotationMeaning
Closurer*Zero or more occurrences of r. Highest precedence
Positive closurer+One or more occurrences, equal to rr*
Concatenationrsr followed by s
Alternationr | sr or s. Lowest precedence

Standard token patterns to be able to write from memory:

letter    →  A | B | ... | Z | a | b | ... | z
digit     →  0 | 1 | ... | 9
id        →  letter ( letter | digit )*
number    →  digit+ ( . digit+ )? ( E (+|-)? digit+ )?
relop     →  < | <= | = | <> | > | >=

DFA against NFA

DFANFA
TransitionsExactly one per state per input symbolZero, one or many per symbol
Epsilon movesNoneAllowed
ConstructionHarder to build from a regular expressionEasy, by Thompson's construction
SpeedFast: one transition per character, no backtrackingSlower: several possibilities must be tracked
SizeCan be exponentially largerCompact
PowerIdentical. Every NFA has an equivalent DFA

That last row is the important one, and it explains the whole toolchain: a scanner generator takes the easy path from a regular expression to an NFA, then converts the NFA to a DFA for speed, then minimises the DFA for size. Regular expression → NFA → DFA → minimal DFA is the pipeline, and naming it in order is often a question by itself.

Drill

  1. Write regular expressions for an identifier and for an unsigned number. As above.
  2. Differentiate a DFA from an NFA. The table, ending on the equivalence of power.
  3. Write a regular expression for strings over {a, b} containing exactly two a's. b* a b* a b*.
  4. Write a regular expression for all strings over {a, b} that end in ab. (a|b)* a b.

t5.prompt: The lexical analyser, or scanner, reads the source character by character, groups the characters into lexemes, and returns a stream of tokens to the parser.
t5.solution:
Its tasks

  • Produce tokens for the parser, on demand: the parser calls the scanner each time it needs the next token.
  • Strip white space and comments, which carry no meaning for the parser.
  • Enter identifiers and constants into the symbol table.
  • Correlate error messages with line numbers, by counting newlines as it goes.
  • Expand macros, where the language has them and there is no separate preprocessor.

Why it is a separate phase

Three reasons, and a question sometimes asks for exactly three: simplicity, since removing white space and comment handling from the parser makes the grammar much smaller; efficiency, since specialised buffering techniques can be applied to character reading alone; and portability, since input device and character set peculiarities are confined to the scanner.

Lexical errors

The scanner detects very little on its own, because almost any character sequence is a plausible lexeme. It catches illegal characters, unterminated strings and comments, and numbers that are too long. Recovery strategies to name: panic mode, deleting characters until a well formed token is found, plus deleting, inserting, replacing or transposing a character.

The one to state clearly: fi (a == b) produces no lexical error at all, because fi is a perfectly valid identifier. Only the parser can notice something is wrong. That example is exactly how examiners test whether you understand the division of labour between the phases.

Drill

  1. State five tasks of a lexical analyser. The five bullets.
  2. Why is lexical analysis separated from parsing? Simplicity, efficiency and portability, with a sentence each.
  3. Give an example of an error the scanner cannot detect and say which phase does. fi (a == b): the scanner returns fi as a valid identifier, and only the parser finds that an identifier cannot begin a statement there.
  4. Name four lexical error recovery strategies. Panic mode deletion, deleting one character, inserting a missing character, replacing or transposing adjacent characters.

t6.prompt: The mechanical conversion at the heart of scanner generation. Each DFA state is a set of NFA states, which is why it is called subset construction.
t6.solution:
The NFA

Take the NFA accepting all strings over {a, b} ending in ab. States q0, q1, q2, start q0, accepting q2:

Stateon aon b
→ q0{q0, q1}{q0}
q1∅{q2}
* q2∅∅

It is non-deterministic because q0 on a goes to two states at once: the machine guesses whether this a is the start of the final ab.

The construction

Start with the set containing the start state and take transitions set by set.

A = {q0}            the start state
A on a  = {q0,q1}   new set, call it B
A on b  = {q0}      = A
B on a  = {q0,q1}   = B
B on b  = {q0,q2}   new set, call it C
C on a  = {q0,q1}   = B
C on b  = {q0}      = A
No new sets appear, so the construction is complete.

The resulting DFA

DFA stateNFA stateson aon bAccepting?
→ A{q0}BANo
B{q0, q1}BCNo
* C{q0, q2}BAYes

A DFA state is accepting if and only if its set contains at least one accepting NFA state. Here C contains q2, so C accepts. State that rule explicitly in the exam; it is a mark.

Where an NFA has epsilon transitions, every set must be replaced by its epsilon closure, which is the set plus everything reachable from it by epsilon moves alone. The start state becomes the closure of {q0}, and after each move the closure is taken again.

Drill

  1. Explain subset construction. Each DFA state is a set of NFA states; begin with the epsilon closure of the start state, and for each set and each input symbol compute the union of the moves and take its closure, adding any new set to the list, until no new sets appear.
  2. Convert the NFA above to a DFA. The worked table, showing every set as it is discovered.
  3. Why can the DFA have exponentially more states than the NFA? Because in the worst case every subset of the NFA's states can be reachable, and a machine with n states has 2n subsets.
  4. What is the epsilon closure of a state? The set of all states reachable from it using epsilon transitions alone, including the state itself.

t7.prompt: How a scanner is actually built in practice, and the two problems that make hand-written scanners awkward.
t7.solution:
Lex and flex

A scanner generator takes a specification of regular expressions with actions and produces the scanner's source code. A lex file has three sections separated by %%: declarations, translation rules, and auxiliary functions.

%{  declarations  %}
%%
[ \t\n]+          { /* skip white space */ }
[0-9]+            { return NUMBER; }
[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9]*  { return IDENTIFIER; }
"+"|"-"|"*"|"/"   { return OPERATOR; }
%%
auxiliary functions

Two rules resolve conflicts when several patterns match: the longest match wins, and if two patterns match the same longest string, the one listed first wins. That second rule is why keywords must be listed above the identifier pattern, or while would be scanned as an identifier.

Input buffering

Reading one character at a time from the file is far too slow, so the scanner reads into a buffer. The standard technique is a pair of buffers of equal size, each filled by one system read, with two pointers: lexemeBegin marking the start of the current lexeme and forward scanning ahead. When forward runs off the end of one half, the other half is refilled. A sentinel character, usually EOF, is placed at the end of each half so that a single test detects both "end of buffer" and "end of file", halving the number of comparisons per character.

Lookahead

The scanner often cannot decide on a token until it has read one character too many. Seeing < it must read the next character to know whether the token is <, <= or <>. That extra character must then be retracted, pushed back so the next token starts in the right place.

The famous case is FORTRAN's DO 5 I = 1.25 against DO 5 I = 1,25: the first is an assignment to a variable called DO5I and the second is a loop, and the scanner cannot tell which until it reaches the comma or the point. It is the standard illustration of why unbounded lookahead is a problem, and it is a memorable example to quote.

Drill

  1. What is a scanner generator, and what are the three sections of a lex specification? A tool that produces scanner code from regular expressions with actions; declarations, translation rules, auxiliary functions.
  2. State the two rules for resolving ambiguity between lex patterns. Longest match wins; on a tie, the earlier listed rule wins.
  3. Why does a scanner use two buffers and a sentinel? Two buffers allow one half to be refilled while the other is still being scanned, so a lexeme spanning the boundary is not lost; the sentinel lets one comparison per character serve as both the end of buffer test and the end of file test.
  4. What is lookahead and why must characters be retracted? Reading beyond the current lexeme to decide which token it is. The extra characters belong to the next token, so the forward pointer must be moved back before scanning resumes.

t8.prompt: The parser takes the token stream and verifies that it can be generated by the grammar of the language, building a parse tree in the process. If it cannot, it reports a syntax error.
t8.solution:
Top down against bottom up

Top downBottom up
Builds the treeFrom the root down to the leavesFrom the leaves up to the root
MethodExpand non-terminals, matching against inputShift tokens onto a stack and reduce by productions
DerivationLeftmostRightmost, produced in reverse
RestrictionGrammar must have no left recursion and no common prefixesHandles a much wider class of grammars
Written byOften by handAlmost always by a generator such as yacc

Error recovery strategies

StrategyWhat it doesCost
Panic modeDiscard tokens until one of a set of synchronising tokens, such as a semicolon or end, is foundSimple and cannot loop forever, but may skip real errors
Phrase levelPerform a local correction on the remaining input, such as inserting a missing semicolonBetter messages, but can loop if the correction is wrong
Error productionsAdd productions to the grammar that match common mistakesExcellent messages, but the errors must be anticipated
Global correctionFind the smallest set of changes turning the input into a legal programTheoretically ideal, too costly in practice

The reason error recovery exists at all is worth one sentence at the start of the answer: without it a compiler would stop at the first mistake, so a program with ten errors would take ten compilations to fix. Recovery lets one run report all of them.

Drill

  1. Differentiate top down from bottom up parsing. The table above.
  2. Name four error recovery strategies with one advantage and one drawback each. The second table.
  3. What are the goals of a good error handler? Report errors clearly and accurately with the location; recover quickly enough to detect later errors; and add little overhead to the compilation of correct programs.

t9.prompt: A predictive parser must choose a production by looking at one token. If two productions for the same non-terminal begin with the same symbols it cannot choose, so the common prefix is factored out and the decision deferred.
t9.solution:
The rule

Given   A → αβ1 | αβ2 | ... | αβn | γ
Replace with
A  → α A' | γ
A' → β1 | β2 | ... | βn

Worked 1: the dangling else

Before:
S → if E then S else S | if E then S | a
The common prefix is "if E then S".
After:
S  → if E then S S' | a
S' → else S | ε

Worked 2

Before:
A → aAB | aBc | aAc
Common prefix a:
A  → a A'
A' → AB | Bc | Ac
A' still has the prefix A in two productions:
A' → A A'' | Bc
A'' → B | c

Note that factoring may need repeating: after one pass a new common prefix can appear, as it does above. Checking for that is the discriminating step in the question.

The dangling else problem itself is worth naming: in if E1 then if E2 then S1 else S2 the else could attach to either if. The universal convention is that an else matches the nearest unmatched then, and grammars are written or parser generators configured to enforce it.

Drill

  1. What is left factoring and why is it needed? Extracting a common prefix from alternative productions so that a predictive parser can defer its choice until the prefix has been consumed, since with one token of lookahead it cannot otherwise decide.
  2. Left factor S → iEtS | iEtSeS | a. S → iEtSS' | a and S' → eS | ε.
  3. Left factor A → ab | abc | abd | b. A → abA' | b, A' → ε | c | d.
  4. Explain the dangling else problem and the usual resolution. As above, with the nearest unmatched then convention.

t10.prompt: A grammar is left recursive if some non-terminal A can derive a string beginning with A. A top down parser meeting E → E + T would call itself on E without consuming any input, and loop forever. So left recursion must be removed before predictive parsing.
t10.solution:
The rule for immediate left recursion

Given   A → Aα1 | Aα2 | ... | Aαm | β1 | β2 | ... | βn
where no βi begins with A
Replace with
A  → β1 A' | β2 A' | ... | βn A'
A' → α1 A' | α2 A' | ... | αm A' | ε

In words: the recursion is turned from left to right, and an epsilon production is added to let it stop.

Worked: the standard expression grammar

Before:
E → E + T | T
T → T * F | F
F → ( E ) | id
For E:  α1 = "+ T",  β1 = "T"
For T:  α1 = "* F",  β1 = "F"
After:
E  → T E'
E' → + T E' | ε
T  → F T'
T' → * F T' | ε
F  → ( E ) | id

This transformed grammar is the one used for every FIRST and FOLLOW example in every textbook, including T11 below. Learn it as a unit; it appears in more exam questions than any other grammar in the course.

Indirect left recursion

Left recursion can hide across several productions:

  S → Aa | b
A → Sc | d
S ⇒ Aa ⇒ Sca   so S is left recursive, indirectly.

The remedy is to substitute until the recursion becomes immediate, then apply the rule above. Substituting S into A gives A → Aac | bc | d, which is immediately left recursive, and the standard rule then yields A → bcA' | dA' with A' → acA' | ε.

Note what is preserved and what is not: the transformed grammar generates exactly the same language, but the parse trees differ in shape, and left recursion is what naturally gives left associativity. That is why removing it is a top down necessity rather than an improvement, and why bottom up parsers, which handle left recursion happily, are preferred for real compilers.

Drill

  1. Why must left recursion be eliminated for top down parsing? Because the parser would expand the non-terminal to itself as the leftmost symbol without consuming any input, recursing infinitely.
  2. Eliminate left recursion from A → Aα | β. A → βA', A' → αA' | ε.
  3. Eliminate left recursion from E → E + T | E − T | T. E → TE', E' → +TE' | −TE' | ε.
  4. Show that S → Aa | b, A → Sc | d is left recursive and remove it. As worked above.

t11.prompt: The biggest calculated question in the course, and the one most worth drilling. Everything follows from two sets and one table-filling rule.
t11.solution:
The rules for FIRST

FIRST(X) is the set of terminals that can begin a string derived from X.

  • If X is a terminal, FIRST(X) = {X}.
  • If X → ε is a production, add ε to FIRST(X).
  • If X → Y1 Y2 ... Yk, add everything in FIRST(Y1) except ε. If FIRST(Y1) contains ε, also add FIRST(Y2) except ε, and so on. If every Yi can derive ε, add ε.

The rules for FOLLOW

FOLLOW(A) is the set of terminals that can appear immediately to the right of A in some derivation.

  • Put $, the end marker, in FOLLOW(S) for the start symbol S.
  • For a production A → αBβ, add FIRST(β) except ε to FOLLOW(B).
  • For A → αB, or A → αBβ where FIRST(β) contains ε, add everything in FOLLOW(A) to FOLLOW(B).

Two mistakes cost most of the marks lost here. ε never goes into a FOLLOW set, only into FIRST sets. And FOLLOW is about what can come after the non-terminal in the whole grammar, so you must look at every production the non-terminal appears in, not just its own.

Worked: the expression grammar from T10

  E  → T E'
E' → + T E' | ε
T  → F T'
T' → * F T' | ε
F  → ( E ) | id

FIRST sets. Work from the bottom up, since F depends on nothing:

FIRST(F)  = { ( , id }
FIRST(T') = { * , ε }
FIRST(T)  = FIRST(F) = { ( , id }        because T → F T'
FIRST(E') = { + , ε }
FIRST(E)  = FIRST(T) = { ( , id }        because E → T E'

FOLLOW sets. Start with the start symbol:

FOLLOW(E)  = { $ }                       E is the start symbol
plus ")" from F → ( E )
= { $ , ) }
FOLLOW(E') = FOLLOW(E)                   from E → T E', E' is last
= { $ , ) }
FOLLOW(T)  = FIRST(E') without ε         from E → T E'
plus FOLLOW(E) because E' can be ε
= { + } ∪ { $ , ) }
= { + , $ , ) }
FOLLOW(T') = FOLLOW(T)                   from T → F T', T' is last
= { + , $ , ) }
FOLLOW(F)  = FIRST(T') without ε         from T → F T'
plus FOLLOW(T) because T' can be ε
= { * } ∪ { + , $ , ) }
= { * , + , $ , ) }

Filling the LL(1) table

For each production A → α: put it in row A under every terminal in FIRST(α). If α can derive ε, also put it under every terminal in FOLLOW(A).

id+*()$
EE → T E'E → T E'
E'E' → + T E'E' → εE' → ε
TT → F T'T → F T'
T'T' → εT' → * F T'T' → εT' → ε
FF → idF → ( E )

A grammar is LL(1) if and only if no cell of the table holds more than one production. Every cell here holds at most one, so this grammar is LL(1). That sentence is the answer to "is this grammar LL(1), and how do you know". Blank cells are error entries, where the parser reports a syntax error.

A left recursive or unfactored grammar produces cells with two entries, which is exactly why T9 and T10 come first. The transformations are not decoration; they are what makes the table well defined.

Drill

  1. State the rules for computing FIRST and FOLLOW. The two bullet lists above.
  2. Compute FIRST and FOLLOW for the grammar S → aBDh, B → cC, C → bC | ε, D → EF, E → g | ε, F → f | ε. Start with FIRST(C) = {b, ε}, FIRST(E) = {g, ε}, FIRST(F) = {f, ε}, then build upward, and take FOLLOW(S) = {$} as the seed.
  3. Construct the LL(1) table for the expression grammar and show it is LL(1). The table above, with the single-entry justification.
  4. Why is ε never in a FOLLOW set? Because FOLLOW is a set of terminals that can actually appear after the non-terminal in a sentential form, and ε is the empty string, not a terminal that can appear anywhere.

t12.prompt: The bottom up method: shift tokens onto a stack until the top of the stack matches the right side of a production, then reduce. Parsing succeeds when the stack holds only the start symbol and the input is exhausted.
t12.solution:
The four actions

  • Shift. Move the next input symbol onto the stack.
  • Reduce. Replace the handle on top of the stack with the non-terminal on the left of its production.
  • Accept. Parsing has succeeded.
  • Error. The input cannot be parsed.

A handle is a substring matching the right side of a production whose reduction represents one step of a rightmost derivation in reverse. Finding the handle is the whole difficulty of bottom up parsing.

Worked: parse id + id * id

Using E → E + E | E * E | id, resolving in favour of the precedence of *:

StackInputAction
$id + id * id $Shift
$ id+ id * id $Reduce by E → id
$ E+ id * id $Shift
$ E +id * id $Shift
$ E + id* id $Reduce by E → id
$ E + E* id $Shift, since * has higher precedence
$ E + E *id $Shift
$ E + E * id$Reduce by E → id
$ E + E * E$Reduce by E → E * E
$ E + E$Reduce by E → E + E
$ E$Accept

The interesting row is the sixth. With E + E on the stack and * next, the parser could reduce E + E to E or shift the *. That is a shift-reduce conflict, and it is resolved by shifting, because * binds tighter than +. Point that row out explicitly in the exam; it shows you know what the table is doing rather than copying steps.

The two conflicts to name

  • Shift-reduce conflict. The parser can either shift or reduce and the grammar does not say which. Usually caused by ambiguity, such as the dangling else. Generators resolve it by shifting.
  • Reduce-reduce conflict. Two different productions could be used to reduce. Generators resolve it by choosing the production listed first, but it usually signals a badly written grammar.

Drill

  1. Define a handle and state the four actions of a shift-reduce parser. As above.
  2. Parse id * id + id by shift-reduce, showing stack, input and action at every step. Same layout as the table above, with the * reduced before the +.
  3. Differentiate a shift-reduce conflict from a reduce-reduce conflict. As above, with a cause and a default resolution for each.
  4. Why is bottom up parsing more powerful than top down? Because the parser postpones its decision until it has seen the whole right side of a production, whereas a top down parser must commit to a production from the lookahead alone. That is why bottom up parsers accept left recursive grammars and a wider class overall.

t13.prompt: The two remaining bottom up techniques on the NOUN outline. Both are usually asked descriptively rather than worked in full, since building an LR table by hand is long.
t13.solution:
Operator precedence parsing

An operator grammar has no production with two adjacent non-terminals on the right side, and no ε production. Operator precedence parsing exploits that by defining three relations between terminals, written a ⋖ b, a ≐ b and a ⋗ b, meaning a yields precedence to b, has the same precedence as b, or takes precedence over b. The handle lies between a ⋖ and the matching ⋗.

It is simple and fast, and it needs only a small table. Its limitations: it applies only to operator grammars, it cannot handle unary minus without a special case since the same token has two meanings, and it may accept strings the grammar does not actually generate.

The LR family

An LR parser uses a stack of states and two tables, ACTION and GOTO. The ACTION table says whether to shift, reduce, accept or error for a given state and lookahead; the GOTO table gives the next state after a reduction.

ParserHow reductions are decidedTable sizePower
LR(0)Reduce whenever a complete item is present, with no lookaheadSmallestWeakest, conflicts are common
SLR(1)Reduce only when the lookahead is in FOLLOW of the left sideSame as LR(0)Better
LALR(1)Merges CLR states having the same coreSame as SLRNearly as strong as CLR; used by yacc and bison
CLR(1)Carries an explicit lookahead in every itemLargest, often many times biggerStrongest

Why LALR(1) is the one used in practice: it has the table size of SLR with almost the power of CLR. That single sentence answers "why do parser generators use LALR" completely.

An item is a production with a dot marking how much has been seen, such as E → E · + T. The set of items reachable at a point becomes one state of the parser, which is how the tables are constructed. Augmenting the grammar means adding S' → S so that acceptance has a unique production to reduce by.

Drill

  1. What is an operator grammar and what are the three precedence relations? No two adjacent non-terminals on any right side and no ε production; the relations ⋖, ≐ and ⋗ between terminals.
  2. State two limitations of operator precedence parsing. It applies only to operator grammars, it mishandles tokens with two meanings such as unary minus, and it can accept strings outside the language.
  3. Compare LR(0), SLR(1), LALR(1) and CLR(1). The table above, closing with why LALR is used in practice.
  4. What is an item, and why is the grammar augmented? A production with a dot showing the position of the parse within it; the grammar is augmented with a new start production so acceptance corresponds to one unique reduction.

t14.prompt: The symbol table is the data structure holding information about every identifier in the source program. It is built by the scanner and parser and consulted by every later phase, which is why it is drawn beside the phases rather than inside one.
t14.solution:
What it stores per identifier

  • The name, the type, and the storage class, such as automatic, static or external.
  • The scope in which it is visible and the memory offset assigned to it.
  • For an array, the number of dimensions and their bounds; for a function, the number and types of parameters and the return type.

Implementations compared

StructureInsertLookupComment
Unordered listO(1)O(n)Simplest, fine only for tiny programs
Ordered listO(n)O(log n) by binary searchInsertion cost makes it awkward
Binary search treeO(log n) averageO(log n) averageDegenerates to O(n) if identifiers arrive in order
Hash tableO(1) averageO(1) averageThe standard choice in real compilers

Scope

A block structured language allows the same name in different scopes, so the table must distinguish them. The usual mechanism is a stack of tables: entering a block pushes a new table, leaving it pops the table, and a lookup searches from the innermost outward. That search order is exactly what implements the rule that an inner declaration hides an outer one.

The two operations to name are insert, which adds a name with its attributes when a declaration is seen, and lookup, which retrieves them when the name is used. A lookup that fails is precisely how "undeclared variable" is detected in semantic analysis.

Drill

  1. What is a symbol table and what information does it hold? The definition and the attribute list above.
  2. Compare four symbol table implementations. The table above, with the hash table as the practical choice.
  3. How does a symbol table handle nested scopes? By a stack of tables pushed on entering a block and popped on leaving, with lookup proceeding from innermost to outermost so inner declarations hide outer ones.
  4. Which phases use the symbol table? All of them: the scanner inserts identifiers, the parser records structure, semantic analysis checks types against it, intermediate and final code generation read offsets and sizes from it.

t15.prompt: Syntax analysis proves the program is well formed; semantic analysis proves it is meaningful. The statement x = y + 1 is syntactically perfect whether or not x and y exist or have compatible types.
t15.solution:
What it checks

  • Type checking. That operands are compatible with their operator and with what they are assigned to.
  • Declaration checking. That every identifier used has been declared, and that none is declared twice in the same scope.
  • Function checks. That the number and types of arguments match the parameters, and that the return type is respected.
  • Flow of control checks. That break or continue appears inside a loop, and that every path returns a value where one is required.
  • Uniqueness checks. That labels and case values are not duplicated.

Static and dynamic checking

Static checks happen at compile time, dynamic checks at run time. Array bounds and division by zero are usually dynamic, because the values are not known until the program runs; type compatibility in a statically typed language is static. The trade-off: static checking catches errors before the program ships and costs nothing at run time, but must be conservative and will reject some programs that would in fact have worked.

Coercion and syntax directed definitions

Coercion is an implicit conversion the compiler inserts, such as the inttoreal in T2. An explicit conversion written by the programmer is a cast.

Semantic rules are usually specified as a syntax directed definition, which attaches attributes to grammar symbols and rules to productions. Synthesised attributes are computed from the children of a node and flow up the tree; inherited attributes are computed from a node's parent or siblings and flow down. The type of an expression is synthesised; the type carried into a list of declared variables is inherited.

That up-and-down distinction is the most examinable thing in this topic, and one example each is enough: E → E1 + E2 synthesises E.type from its two children, while D → T L passes T.type down into L as an inherited attribute so every identifier in the list gets it.

Drill

  1. What is semantic analysis, and name four checks it performs. The definition and any four bullets.
  2. Differentiate static from dynamic checking, with an example of each. Compile time against run time; type compatibility against array bounds.
  3. Differentiate synthesised from inherited attributes. Computed from children and flowing up, against computed from parent or siblings and flowing down, with the two examples above.
  4. Differentiate coercion from casting. Coercion is inserted implicitly by the compiler; a cast is written explicitly by the programmer.

t16.prompt: Three address code is the standard intermediate representation: each instruction has at most one operator and at most three addresses, two operands and a result. Complex expressions are broken up using compiler-generated temporaries.
t16.solution:
Why an intermediate representation at all

  • It is machine independent, so one optimiser serves every target.
  • It decouples front end from back end, giving the m + n saving of T1.
  • It is easy to optimise, because each instruction does exactly one thing.
  • It can be reordered and rewritten safely, since dependencies are explicit.

Worked 1: an arithmetic expression

Source:   a = b * c + b * d
Three address code:
t1 = b * c
t2 = b * d
t3 = t1 + t2
a  = t3
After common subexpression elimination is not possible here,
since b*c and b*d differ. But if the source were a = b*c + b*c:
t1 = b * c
t2 = t1 + t1
a  = t2

Worked 2: a conditional

Source:   if (a < b) x = 1; else x = 2;
Three address code:
100:  if a < b goto 103
101:  x = 2
102:  goto 104
103:  x = 1
104:  ...

Worked 3: a loop

Source:   while (i < n) { s = s + i; i = i + 1; }
Three address code:
100:  if i < n goto 102
101:  goto 105
102:  s = s + i
103:  i = i + 1
104:  goto 100
105:  ...

The three representations

For a = b * c + d, with t1 = b * c then t2 = t1 + d then a = t2:

Quadruplesoparg1arg2result
0*bct1
1+t1dt2
2=t2a
Triplesoparg1arg2
(0)*bc
(1)+(0)d
(2)=a(1)

The difference and why it matters: quadruples name an explicit temporary, triples refer to an instruction by its position. So triples are more compact but cannot be reordered, because moving an instruction changes the positions every other instruction refers to. Quadruples can be moved freely, which is why optimising compilers prefer them. Indirect triples are the compromise: a separate list of pointers to triples, so reordering the pointer list moves instructions without touching the triples.

The other intermediate forms to name are the syntax tree, the directed acyclic graph which shares repeated subexpressions, and postfix notation.

Drill

  1. What is three address code and why is an intermediate representation used? The definition and the four reasons above.
  2. Write three address code for x = (a + b) * (c - d) / e. t1 = a + b; t2 = c − d; t3 = t1 * t2; t4 = t3 / e; x = t4.
  3. Write three address code for for (i = 0; i < 10; i++) sum = sum + i; Initialise i = 0, label the test, conditional jump past the body when it fails, body, increment, jump back to the test.
  4. Differentiate quadruples from triples. As above, ending on the reordering point and indirect triples.

t17.prompt: Optimisation works on basic blocks: maximal sequences of instructions entered only at the first and left only at the last, so that if the first runs, all of them run in order.
t17.solution:
Finding basic blocks

First identify the leaders, then each block runs from a leader to just before the next. An instruction is a leader if it is:

  1. The first instruction of the program.
  2. The target of any conditional or unconditional jump.
  3. The instruction immediately following a jump.

The flow graph then has one node per basic block, with an edge from block B1 to B2 if control can pass directly from the end of B1 to the start of B2. It is the structure every global optimisation is computed over, and loops are found in it as cycles.

Applying it to the loop from T16

   100:  if i < n goto 102      leader: first instruction
101:  goto 105               leader: follows a jump
102:  s = s + i              leader: target of a jump
103:  i = i + 1
104:  goto 100
105:  ...                    leader: target of a jump
Blocks:  B1 = {100}   B2 = {101}   B3 = {102,103,104}   B4 = {105}
Edges:   B1 → B3 (branch taken), B1 → B2 (fall through)
B2 → B4,  B3 → B1 (the loop back edge)

The edge B3 → B1 is the back edge, and a back edge is precisely what identifies a loop in the flow graph. Since loops dominate execution time, they are where optimisation pays, which is why loop invariant code motion and strength reduction matter more than anything done to straight line code.

The techniques themselves are in R5 with an example each. Optimisation is classified as local within one basic block, global across blocks using flow analysis, and peephole, a small sliding window over the generated code removing redundant loads, jumps to jumps and unreachable instructions.

Drill

  1. Define a basic block and state the three rules for finding leaders. As above.
  2. Construct the flow graph for a given three address code fragment. Find the leaders, split into blocks, then draw an edge wherever control can flow directly.
  3. Differentiate local, global and peephole optimisation. Within one block, across blocks using data flow analysis, and over a small window of the final code.
  4. Why do optimisers concentrate on loops? Because a loop body executes many times, so removing one instruction from it saves that cost on every iteration, while the same saving in straight line code is made once.

t18.prompt: The final phase turns optimised intermediate code into target code. Its three jobs are instruction selection, register allocation and instruction ordering.
t18.solution:
The issues in code generation

IssueThe problem
Input formWhich intermediate representation the generator consumes, and whether it is still machine independent
Target programAbsolute machine code, relocatable machine code, or assembly language
Memory managementMapping names to run time addresses, using the symbol table offsets
Instruction selectionChoosing instructions of the right cost. A naive one-to-one translation gives correct but poor code
Register allocationDeciding which values live in registers, since register operations are far faster than memory ones
Evaluation orderChoosing an order that needs fewest registers and fewest spills

Register allocation is the hardest of the six and the one to say something substantial about: registers are the fastest storage and there are very few of them, so the generator must decide which values to keep and which to spill to memory. Choosing optimally is NP-complete, so real compilers use heuristics, the best known modelling it as graph colouring where each value is a node, an edge joins values live at the same time, and the colours are the registers.

Run time storage

Three allocation strategies, and which language features force each:

  • Static allocation. Addresses fixed at compile time. Simple, but no recursion and no dynamic sizes.
  • Stack allocation. An activation record, or stack frame, is pushed per call holding parameters, local variables, the return address and saved registers. This is what makes recursion possible, since each invocation gets its own frame.
  • Heap allocation. For data whose lifetime does not follow the call structure, such as anything explicitly allocated and freed by the program.

Peephole optimisation on the generated code

A final pass over a small window catches what earlier phases could not see: redundant load and store pairs, jumps to jumps, unreachable code, and algebraic simplifications such as multiplying by one or adding zero.

Before:              After:
MOV R0, a            MOV R0, a
MOV a, R0            (removed: it stores back what was just loaded)

Drill

  1. State six issues in the design of a code generator. The table above.
  2. Why is register allocation difficult? Registers are the fastest storage and are very scarce, values must be spilled when they run out, and choosing the optimal assignment is NP-complete, so heuristics such as graph colouring are used.
  3. Differentiate static, stack and heap allocation, and say which supports recursion. As above; stack allocation supports recursion because each activation gets its own record.
  4. What is peephole optimisation? Give two examples. A pass over a small sliding window of target code replacing short sequences with better ones: removing a store that immediately follows the matching load, and replacing a jump to a jump with a direct jump.

p1.prompt:
(a) Show the parsing sequences (derivations) for (A+B)*(C/D) and B*C-D. (6)

(b) Using two-column stacks, obtain the parse tree of the two expressions. (7)

(c) For A*B+C*D+E/F*(G-H)-(I-J-K*L)*(M*N-O/P): (i) generate code using the elementary algorithm (4); (ii) draw the tree and generate code using the tree algorithm (8).
p1.solution:
(a) Leftmost derivations

(A+B)*(C/D), expanding the leftmost non-terminal each step:

E ⇒ T ⇒ T*F ⇒ F*F ⇒ (E)*F ⇒ (E+T)*F ⇒ (T+T)*F
⇒ (F+T)*F ⇒ (A+T)*F ⇒ (A+F)*F ⇒ (A+B)*F
⇒ (A+B)*(E) ⇒ (A+B)*(T) ⇒ (A+B)*(T/F)
⇒ (A+B)*(F/F) ⇒ (A+B)*(C/F) ⇒ (A+B)*(C/D)

B*C-D:

E ⇒ E-T ⇒ T-T ⇒ T*F-T ⇒ F*F-T ⇒ B*F-T
⇒ B*C-T ⇒ B*C-F ⇒ B*C-D

(b) Parse trees

The two-column stack parse is bottom-up: read left to right, shift onto the stack, and reduce by a production whenever the top matches a right-hand side. The tree it builds for each:

(A+B)*(C/D)              B*C-D
E                    E
|                  / | \
T                 E  -  T
/ | \               |     |
T  *  F              T      F
|    /|\           / | \    |
F   ( E )         T  *  F   D
/|\    |           |     |
( E )  T/F          F     C
|    ...          |
E+T   C,D          B

Read the left tree top down: the root is a product (T*F); its left is (A+B), a parenthesised sum; its right is (C/D), a parenthesised quotient. The right tree makes B*C a single T before the subtraction, which is why * binds tighter than -.

(c) Code generation

(i) Elementary algorithm. Scan the expression in precedence order and emit one three-address instruction, with a fresh temporary, for every operator. For A*B+C*D+E/F*(G-H)-(I-J-K*L)*(M*N-O/P):

t1  = A * B
t2  = C * D
t3  = t1 + t2
t4  = E / F
t5  = G - H
t6  = t4 * t5
t7  = t3 + t6
t8  = I - J
t9  = K * L
t10 = t8 - t9
t11 = M * N
t12 = O / P
t13 = t11 - t12
t14 = t10 * t13
t15 = t7 - t14      ; final result

(ii) Tree algorithm. Build the syntax tree, then generate code by a postorder traversal: emit code for a node's children before the node itself, so an operator's operands are always ready. The instructions come out in exactly the order above (t1 through t15), because postorder on the expression tree visits multiplications and divisions before the additions and subtractions that combine them. The advantage of the tree form is that it exposes structure for optimisation: a temporary can be reused once its value is consumed (Sethi-Ullman register numbering minimises how many are live at once), and any repeated subtree can be computed once. The elementary algorithm cannot see that; the tree can.

p2.prompt: (a) List any five reserved words of your choice and draw the transition diagram. (5) (b) Write state programs to implement any five states in (a). (5) (c) Obtain the triples for Z = (M+N)*(O+P)/((Q+R)*(S+T)/(U+V)). (5)
p2.solution:
(a) Reserved words and transition diagram

Five reserved words: if, then, else, begin, end. A transition diagram recognises them letter by letter from a start state, branching on the next character. Sketch, from start state s0:

s0 --i--> s1 --f--> [IF]
s0 --t--> s2 --h--> s3 --e--> s4 --n--> [THEN]
s0 --e--> s5 --l--> s6 --s--> s7 --e--> [ELSE]

s0 --e--> s5 --n--> s12 --d--> [END]

Accepting states in brackets return the token. In practice the scanner reads the whole identifier, then looks it up in a reserved-word table, which is simpler than a separate branch per keyword.

(b) State programs

Each state becomes a labelled routine that reads the next character and jumps to the next state, following the classic scanner idiom:

state0: c = nextchar();
if (c=='i') goto state1;
if (c=='t') goto state2;
... else goto other;

The same shape (read, test, goto, or retract on mismatch) implements states 2 through 5.

(c) Triples for Z = (M+N)*(O+P)/((Q+R)*(S+T)/(U+V))

A triple is (operator, arg1, arg2) with no result name; other triples refer to a result by its index (in parentheses).

p3.prompt: (a) Define intermediate code and state why we change to intermediate form before code generation. (4) (b) For the CIRCLE program segment: (i) list the tokens (3); (ii) show the uniform symbol table (3). (c) Obtain the quadruples for Z = K*((A+B)-C*D)-E*F/(G-H+I*J). (5)
p3.solution:
(a) Intermediate code

Intermediate code is a representation between the source and the target machine code, independent of both, for example three-address code or a syntax tree. We use it because it decouples the front end from the back end: one front end per language and one back end per machine can be mixed and matched (m + n pieces instead of m×n compilers). It is also the natural place to apply machine-independent optimisation, and it keeps the compiler portable and retargetable.

(b) Tokens and symbol table

p4.solution:
Read the bracketing off your own copy These two questions use long expressions that are easy to mis-transcribe. The answers below are for the expressions exactly as printed here; if your paper brackets one differently, apply the same method to yours.

(a) Prefix (operator before operands)

(c) Bottom-up (shift-reduce) parse of (A+B)+(C+D*E)

Keep a stack; shift the next input symbol, or reduce the top of the stack by a production. Handles are reduced as soon as they appear.

StackInputAction

$E+T$reduce E→E+T
$E$accept

Inside the second bracket, D*E reduces to a single T (via T→T*F) before the +, so C+D*E parses as C+(D*E). The stack collapses to E with empty input, so the string is accepted.

p5.prompt: (a) Draw the parse tree for A+B*C+D+E*F-(G*H+I+J*K)*L. (5) (b) Show the operator precedence table for |- ( ) + - * / ^ -|. (5) (c) Lexical analysis could be folded into syntax analysis. Give three reasons for keeping the phases separate. (5)
p5.solution:
(a) Parse tree for A+B*C+D+E*F-(G*H+I+J*K)*L

Because * binds tighter than + and -, and +/- are left-associative, the expression groups as ((((A+(B*C))+D)+(E*F)) - ((G*H+I+J*K)*L)). Its three-address form makes the shape explicit:

t1  = B * C
t2  = A + t1
t3  = t2 + D
t4  = E * F
t5  = t3 + t4
t6  = G * H
t7  = t6 + I
t8  = J * K
t9  = t7 + t8
t10 = t9 * L
t11 = t5 - t10     ; root of the tree

The tree's root is the final subtraction (t11); its left subtree is the running sum t5, its right subtree is the parenthesised product t10. Each * sits below the +/- that uses it.

(b) Operator-precedence table

Operator precedence uses three relations: a <. b (a yields to b), a .> b (a takes precedence), and a =. b (equal, as in ( and )). They are set from two rules: the higher-precedence operator wins on either side, and for equal precedence a left-associative operator takes precedence over itself (.>), while the right-associative ^ yields to itself (<.). Precedence order high to low: ^, then * /, then + -. The markers |- (start) and -| (end) sit below everything.

+ -* /^()id-|
+ -.><.<.<..><..>
* /.>.><.<..><..>
^.>.><.<..><..>
(<.<.<.<.=.<.
).>.>.>.>.>
id.>.>.>.>.>
|-<.<.<.<.<.=.

Blank cells are error entries: that pair can never legally sit adjacent. |- =. -| marks a completely reduced input.

(c) Why keep lexical and syntax analysis separate

  • Simpler design: separating the two lets the scanner use simple regular expressions/finite automata while the parser uses context-free grammars, so neither is burdened with the other's job.
  • Efficiency: the scanner can use fast, specialised techniques (buffering, table-driven DFAs) on the character stream, which would slow a parser down if merged.
  • Portability and maintainability: machine or character-set specifics (whitespace, comments, encodings) are confined to the scanner, so the parser stays clean and either phase can change without disturbing the other.

p6.prompt: (a) Using the Question One grammar, show the parse with semantic action for A*B-C/D-A+B-C*D+B. (6) (b) Write productions for, assuming integer arithmetic: (i) an if statement, (ii) an assignment statement, (iii) a read statement. (6) (c) A language is left-recursive if a production A → Aα exists. Discuss. (3)
p6.solution:
(a) Parse with semantic actions

A semantic action is code attached to a production that runs on reduction; here each action emits three-address code and returns a temporary. Bottom-up over A*B-C/D-A+B-C*D+B (left-associative, *// first):

reduce A*B   {t1 = A * B}
reduce C/D   {t2 = C / D}
reduce t1-t2 {t3 = t1 - t2}
reduce t3-A  {t4 = t3 - A}
reduce t4+B  {t5 = t4 + B}
reduce C*D   {t6 = C * D}
reduce t5-t6 {t7 = t5 - t6}
reduce t7+B  {t8 = t7 + B}   ; value of the expression

Each +/- action fires only after both its operands are reduced, which is why C*D is computed (t6) before the subtraction that uses it.

(b) Grammar productions

(i)   S → if ( C ) then S
| if ( C ) then S else S
C → E relop E          (relop: < | > | == | ...)
(ii)  S → id := E
E → E + T | E - T | T
T → T * F | T / F | F
F → ( E ) | id | num
(iii) S → read ( id )

With only integer arithmetic, num is an integer literal and E produces an integer-valued expression, so no type coercion rules are needed.

(c) Left recursion

A grammar is left-recursive when a non-terminal can derive a string that begins with itself, as in A → Aα (immediate) or through a chain (indirect). It is natural for expressing left-associative operators, and works fine for bottom-up (LR) parsers. But it is fatal for top-down (recursive-descent, LL) parsers: the parser would call A to match A before consuming any input and loop forever. So left recursion must be eliminated before top-down parsing, by rewriting A → Aα | β as A → βA', A' → αA' | ε, which accepts the same language without the self-first reference.

pb1.prompt: (a)(i) State and explain two low-level languages. (ii) Give the corresponding binary of the assembly LOAD TEMP; MPY VALUE; STORE PROD. (b) Write a FORTRAN IV program to add two variables; (i) its token representation from lexical analysis. (c) Role of error diagnostics in the pre-processor; (i) the units by which compilation begins scanning.
pb1.solution:
(a) Low-level languages

(i) Two LLLs: Machine language, pure binary instructions the CPU runs directly, and Assembly language, mnemonic names (LOAD, ADD) for those instructions, one-to-one with machine code but human-readable and needing an assembler to translate.

(ii) Each mnemonic has an opcode; the operand is an address. So LOAD TEMP becomes opcode(LOAD) | address(TEMP), MPY VALUE becomes opcode(MPY) | address(VALUE), STORE PROD becomes opcode(STORE) | address(PROD). For example with 4-bit opcodes LOAD=0001, MPY=0010, STORE=0011 and TEMP/VALUE/PROD at addresses 1000/1001/1010: 0001 1000, 0010 1001, 0011 1010. The exact bits depend on the machine's opcode table; the point is opcode followed by operand address.

(b) FORTRAN and its tokens

      PROGRAM ADD
INTEGER A, B, C
READ *, A, B
C = A + B
PRINT *, C
END

(i) Tokens from C = A + B: identifier C, operator =, identifier A, operator +, identifier B. Across the program the lexical analyser produces keyword tokens (PROGRAM, INTEGER, READ, PRINT, END), identifiers (ADD, A, B, C), operators (=, +, *) and punctuation (comma).

(c) Pre-processor and scanning units

Error diagnostics in the pre-processor catch and report faults before compilation proper: undefined macros, bad #include files, malformed directives. Catching them early gives clear messages and stops a cascade of misleading errors later.

(i) Units of scanning: compilation begins by grouping characters into lexemes, which are classified into tokens (the smallest meaningful units: identifiers, keywords, operators, literals). The scanner also skips the non-tokens: whitespace and comments.

pb2.prompt: (a) Compare grammar G and language L(G). (i) Explain BNF as it relates to grammar. (b) Difference between a sentence and a language. (i) Four possible sentences from "Man, the, House, has". (c) What is Chomsky classification? (i) Explain the recursive states of a language.
pb2.solution:
(a) Grammar vs language, and BNF

A grammar G is the finite set of rules (a 4-tuple of non-terminals, terminals, productions and a start symbol) that defines a language. The language L(G) is the possibly infinite set of all strings those rules can generate. In short, G is the rulebook; L(G) is everything the rulebook produces.

(i) BNF (Backus-Naur Form) is a notation for writing context-free grammars: <non-terminal> ::= expansion, with | for alternatives. Example <expr> ::= <expr> + <term> | <term>. It is the standard way to specify a programming language's syntax.

(b) Sentence vs language

A sentence is a single string of terminals derivable from the start symbol; a language is the set of all such sentences. One sentence is a member; the language is the whole collection.

(i) From the words {Man, the, House, has}, four grammatical sentences: "The Man has the House", "The House has the Man", "The Man has House", "Man has the House". (The exact set depends on the toy grammar; any well-formed orderings score.)

(c) Chomsky classification, recursion

Chomsky hierarchy classifies grammars by the form of their productions into four types, each more restricted than the last:

TypeGrammarRecogniser
0unrestrictedTuring machine
1context-sensitivelinear-bounded automaton
2context-freepushdown automaton
3regularfinite automaton

(i) Recursion in a grammar: a production is left-recursive (A → Aα), right-recursive (A → αA), or self-embedding (A → αAβ). Recursion is what lets a finite grammar generate infinitely many, arbitrarily long sentences; left recursion in particular must be removed for top-down parsing (see 2024/25 Q6c).

pb3.prompt: (a) Differentiate the three ends of the compiler. (i) Who is a developer, and what is a deadly sin in development? (b) Define: (i) peephole optimisation, (ii) common subexpression, (iii) loop jamming. (c) Compare compiler and interpreter.
pb3.solution:
(a) The ends of a compiler

A compiler splits into phases usually grouped as two (or three) ends:

  • Front end: analysis. Lexical, syntax and semantic analysis plus intermediate-code generation. Depends on the source language, not the machine.
  • Middle end: machine-independent optimisation of the intermediate code.
  • Back end: synthesis. Code generation and machine-dependent optimisation. Depends on the target machine, not the source language.

(i) A developer writes and maintains the software. A "deadly sin" in development is, for instance, skipping error handling and testing (or ignoring optimisation and documentation), because it produces code that is unreliable and unmaintainable.

(b) Optimisation terms

  • Peephole optimisation: a local pass over a small sliding window of target instructions, replacing short inefficient sequences with better ones (removing a redundant load, folding constants).
  • Common subexpression: an expression computed more than once whose operands do not change between uses, so it can be computed once and reused (elimination).
  • Loop jamming (fusion): merging two adjacent loops that iterate over the same range into one, saving loop overhead.

(c) Compiler vs interpreter

CompilerInterpreter
Translationwhole program to machine code, oncestatement by statement, at run time
Execution speedfaster (pre-translated)slower (translates each run)
Errorsreported after full compilationreported at the first faulty line, then stops
Outputa standalone executableno separate executable
ExampleC, C++Python, BASIC

pb4.prompt: (a) The code that is neither source nor object code. (i) Examples. (b) Compare dead code and redundant code. (i) Three-address code for (a-b)/(c+d). (c) Is code optimisation necessary? Justify.
pb4.solution:
(a) Code that is neither source nor object

That is intermediate code: a representation the compiler uses internally, lower than the source but higher than machine code, and independent of the target. (i) Examples: three-address code, quadruples and triples, postfix (reverse Polish) notation, syntax trees and DAGs, and bytecode.

(b) Dead code vs redundant code

Dead code is code whose result is never used, or that can never be reached (a statement after a return, an assignment to a variable that is never read). Redundant code computes something already available, repeating work whose result exists (recomputing a common subexpression). Dead code can be deleted outright; redundant code is replaced by a reference to the existing value.

(i) Three-address code for (a-b)/(c+d):

t1 = a - b
t2 = c + d
t3 = t1 / t2

(c) Is optimisation necessary?

Yes, though not strictly required for correctness. An unoptimised compiler still produces working code, so optimisation is not mandatory. But it is highly desirable: it makes programs run faster, use less memory, and consume less power, which matters on constrained or heavily used systems. The justification is a trade-off: optimisation costs compile time and compiler complexity, and must never change the program's meaning, so it is applied where the runtime payoff is worth that cost.

pb5.prompt: (a) What is a DAG? Its advantages in optimisation. (i) What is three-address code? (b) Construct a DAG and three-address code for a + a*(b-c) + (b-c)*d. (c) Three-address code for a = b*-c + b*-c, and implement with quadruples and triples.
pb5.solution:
(a) DAG and three-address code

A DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) is a syntax tree in which identical subexpressions are shared rather than duplicated: a repeated computation appears as one node with several parents. Its advantage in optimisation is that it exposes common subexpressions (compute once), reveals dead code (nodes no parent uses), and shows how many times each value is used, guiding register allocation.

(i) Three-address code is intermediate code where each instruction has at most three operands, typically x = y op z, so every computed value gets a name.

(b) DAG and code for a + a*(b-c) + (b-c)*d

The subexpression (b-c) appears twice, so the DAG computes it once (node t1) and both users point at it:

DAG (shared node t1 = b-c):
+            t1 = b - c        (computed ONCE)
/ \           t2 = a * t1
+   *d         t4 = t1 * d       (reuses t1)
/ \  |
a  *  t1 ........shared
|
a,t1

Optimised three-address code from the DAG (four temporaries, not five, because b-c is shared):

t1 = b - c
t2 = a * t1
t3 = a + t2
t4 = t1 * d
t5 = t3 + t4

A naive tree would recompute b-c a second time; the DAG saves that instruction. That saving is the whole point of the DAG.

(c) a = b*-c + b*-c

-c is unary minus, and b*-c occurs twice. Three-address code (naive):

t1 = - c
t2 = b * t1
t3 = - c
t4 = b * t3
t5 = t2 + t4
a  = t5

Quadruples (op, arg1, arg2, result):

#oparg1arg2result
1uminusct1
2*bt1t2
3uminusct3
4*bt3t4
5+t2t4t5
6=t5a

Triples (op, arg1, arg2), referenced by index:

#oparg1arg2
(0)uminusc
(1)*b(0)
(2)uminusc
(3)*b(2)
(4)+(1)(3)
(5)=a(4)

Common-subexpression elimination would drop triples (2) and (3), reusing (1) for both, since b*-c is the same value both times.

pb6.prompt: (a)(i) Local vs global optimisation. (ii) What is UD chaining? (b) Define, for UD chaining: (i) USE, (ii) GEN[B], (iii) KILL[B], (iv) IN. (c) Applications of UD-chains. (i) Types of optimisation for the dot-product loop.
pb6.solution:
(a) Local vs global, and UD chaining

(i) Local optimisation works within a single basic block (a straight-line run with no branches in or out). Global optimisation works across basic blocks, over the whole control-flow graph, and so needs data-flow analysis.

(ii) UD chaining (use-definition chaining) links each use of a variable to all the definitions that could have produced the value reaching it. It is a data-flow analysis that underpins many global optimisations.

(b) UD-chaining terms for a block B

  • USE: a point where a variable's value is read.
  • GEN[B]: the definitions made inside B that reach the end of B (generated and still live at exit).
  • KILL[B]: the definitions elsewhere that B overwrites, so they no longer reach past B.
  • IN[B]: the set of definitions reaching the entry of B (from all its predecessors).

The reaching-definitions equation ties them together: OUT[B] = GEN[B] ∪ (IN[B] − KILL[B]).

(c) Applications, and the dot-product loop

Applications of UD-chains: reaching-definitions analysis, dead-code elimination, constant propagation, loop-invariant code motion, and detecting uninitialised uses.

(i) Optimising the dot-product loop (PROD accumulates X[I]*Y[I] for I=1..5):

  • Strength reduction and common-subexpression elimination on the array addressing: the offsets for X[I] and Y[I] are recomputed each pass; compute the addresses incrementally instead of by a fresh multiplication.
  • Loop-invariant code motion: anything inside the loop that does not change (base addresses, the constant bound) is hoisted out.
  • Induction-variable elimination: I is a simple induction variable; replace repeated I := I + 1 plus index arithmetic with a single pointer that steps by the element size.
  • Register allocation: keep PROD and the loop index in registers across iterations rather than reloading them.
